description: ASTRO LABS is a student-led team from Van, Türkiye, joining NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in space exploration, mobile software, game development, design, and data analysis. Our goal is to create innovative solutions by combining science, creativity, and technology. We welcome teammates interested in coding, research, and teamwork.
summary: ASTRO VITAL is a health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. It brings live vital signs, crew check-ins, hydration, sleep, exercise and real space-radiation data into one console, and maps them to NASA's five human spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, hostile closed environment). Every reading gets a clear status (NOMINAL, WATCH or ACT) and a concrete next action, so astronauts can evaluate and act on their own health when the delay to Earth makes ground support slow. A Mission Control view lets the flight surgeon follow the whole crew, review deviations and leave notes. Live scenarios (solar storm during a spacewalk, cabin CO2 rise, heart-rate spike) show how the system reacts and guides the crew back to safety.
details:
What it does: ASTRO VITAL is a health-monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. It has two roles. The astronaut side shows a live console: an astronaut figure on the right, and on the left boxes for biometrics (heart rate, SpO2, respiration, skin temperature, blood pressure, HRV, stress, reaction time), an ECG and pulse waveform, a radiation dosimeter, a five-hazard radar and cabin air. Around it are screens for daily check-in (sleep, energy, mood, symptoms), hydration, health trends, exercise, the mission timeline and notes from the health team. The Mission Control side shows every crew member, flags deviations from personal baselines, lists reviews to approve, compares astronauts and exports reports.

How it works: A live data layer ticks every second. The ISS position is polled from a public API every five seconds and drawn on an orbit map; when the station passes over the South Atlantic Anomaly the dose rate rises and the crew is warned. The radiation dose comes from a real NASA OSDR RadLab DosTel1 record from the ISS (1-2 April 2022, 596 records, about 0.36 mGy per day, SAA peak about 558 uGy/h), replayed in order. Every value is compared with the astronaut's own pre-mission baseline and mapped to one of NASA's five human spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity, hostile closed environment). Each reading gets a status (NOMINAL, WATCH or ACT) and a concrete next action, such as moving to a shielded area, changing the CO2 scrubber cartridge or drinking water. Scenario buttons start short animated stories: in a solar storm during a spacewalk, the dose and stress rise and a "Return to base" button brings the astronaut back inside, after which the values recover.

Benefits and impact: On the way to Mars a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes one way, so astronauts must notice health changes and act on their own. ASTRO VITAL gives them one clear picture and the next step, without waiting for the ground. The flight surgeon still sees the whole crew and problems early. The same approach can help analog habitats, polar stations and other remote teams. Vital signs in the demo are simulated for a fictional crew and clearly labelled; no real personal health data is used.

Creativity: Instead of only showing numbers, every alert is tied to a NASA hazard and to an action. Values are judged against each person's own baseline, not a population average. Animated scenarios make the system easy to understand and useful for training. Every panel shows whether its data is LIVE, NASA or SIMULATED.

Tools: Flutter and Dart (one codebase for Android, iOS, web and desktop), http, fl_chart, flutter_svg, shared_preferences and share_plus.

Use of AI: OpenAI Codex helped us build the first prototype. Anthropic's Claude helped write and refactor the Flutter code, generate the SVG astronaut illustrations and the cover image, and draft the English texts and the demo video. ChatGPT helped us research NASA hazards and astronaut health indicators. Our team chose the features, checked the data against the NASA sources, tested the app and made the final decisions. AI-assisted images and the video carry an "AI-assisted" mark, every AI-assisted source file starts with a comment saying so, and the README explains which parts were made with AI help.

Team: ASTRO LABS, Van, Turkiye.
